messages.content:
You are an evidence extraction specialist for PFAS treatment and remediation
research. Build a structured study evidence table before any narrative review
is written.

Extract one record per primary-study experiment, modeled scenario, or field
deployment that contributes usable evidence to the review task. A paper may
produce more than one record only when materially different matrices,
technologies, operating regimes, or endpoints would otherwise be conflated.

Review articles and perspectives may help identify terminology or primary
studies, but they must not be used as the source of a quantitative study
record. Never copy a review table as though it were a primary result.

For every populated source-dependent field:
- preserve the PFAS identity or class, matrix, starting concentration or
  loading, operating conditions, study scale, measured endpoint, value, unit,
  and material qualifiers when reported;
- attach only the field-level evidence locator identifiers that directly
  support that specific value or statement;
- use an empty string or empty array when the source does not report the
  information; do not infer or estimate it;
- do not turn the absence of information in the supplied packet into a study
  finding, quantitative result, or author-reported limitation unless the source
  explicitly states that absence;
- distinguish removal, separation, sorption, parent-compound loss,
  transformation, degradation, destruction, defluorination, mineralization,
  total organofluorine change, and toxicity change;
- classify endpoint_type from what was actually measured, not from the
  authors' preferred label. Parent loss alone is not destruction. Phase
  transfer is removal or separation, not degradation. Inorganic fluoride
  release or fluorine-balance closure can establish defluorination but cannot
  by itself establish mineralization. Use mineralization only when direct
  carbon-fate evidence such as CO2/inorganic-carbon production or a carbon
  balance is reported. Preserve a broader author term in reported_term and
  explain any mismatch in interpretation;
- do not normalize or compare values unless their units, denominators,
  matrices, PFAS scope, operating conditions, and endpoints permit it.

Only populate quantitative_findings when the source reports an actual numeric
value, inequality, approximate value, range, or explicit ND/not-detected
result. Put the number or censoring marker in value and the measurement unit in
unit. Normalize Unicode inequality signs to ASCII >= or <= and range dashes to
an ASCII hyphen while preserving the source wording in qualifiers. A unit or
order-of-magnitude scale without a number is not a quantitative finding.
Qualitative parent loss, intermediate formation, or disappearance belongs in
the endpoint interpretation or residual/byproduct statements instead.

Set value_form to exactly one of:
- exact_numeric: a bare number such as `99.7` or `1.2e-3`;
- approximate_numeric: `~` followed by a number;
- inequality: `<`, `<=`, `>`, or `>=` followed by a number;
- range: two numbers separated by `-` or `to`; or
- not_detected: exactly `ND`, `N/D`, `not detected`,
  `below detection limit`, or `below quantification limit`.

Put uncertainty, denominators, fold-change wording, and explanatory text in
qualifiers rather than value. A deterministic validator will remove malformed
quantitative fields before source verification.

For limitations, use basis=author_reported only when the source states the
limitation. Use basis=design_inferred only for a constraint that follows
directly from cited design evidence, such as one matrix, one compound, or
bench-scale operation. Never label missing information in the supplied packet
as a scientific limitation of the study.

Mark each record as comparable with conditions, descriptive only, or not
comparable. Comparability is an analyst inference rather than a quotation:
attach locators for the matrix, scale, conditions, endpoint, and denominator
on which the inference rests, and explain the reason. Do not reward a study
for reporting a larger percentage when its endpoint or conditions differ.

The task was derived from a defining review that is held out from all
candidate retrieval systems. The supplied anchor identifiers are an exclusion
list, not evidence. Do not extract from the anchor, cite it, reconstruct its
conclusions, or use its tables.

Return one JSON object that follows the supplied evidence-table schema exactly.
Do not write the narrative review in this step.

records.citation: Griffin, A.M.; Elbers, J.; Bellona, C.; Strathmann, T.J. Combining Nanofiltration and Adsorbents to Achieve Effective PFAS Removal in Wastewater Effluent. Environ. Sci. Technol. 2026. DOI: 10.1021/acs.est.5c17011.

comparability.reason: The record reports PFAS rejection percentages for a defined membrane (NF270), water matrix (tertiary wastewater effluent), and operating recovery (90%) at pilot scale, with clear identification of PFAS classes. These conditions and endpoints allow comparison to other membrane studies that report rejection/removal for specified PFAS in wastewater or similar matrices, provided differences in membrane tightness, matrix composition, and recovery are accounted for.

endpoints.interpretation: NF270 achieved high rejection of most PFAS in tertiary wastewater at 90% recovery: >92% for C >= 4 PFAAs, >98% for Gen-X, and 63-92% for ultrashort-chain PFAS; rejection values remained stable over 45 days despite permeability loss due to fouling/scaling.

The loose NF270 membrane was used as an initial step to reduce EfOM and selected inorganic ions that interfere with downstream PFAS adsorption by GAC and IX, thereby improving overall treatment-train PFAS removal performance.
endpoints.reported_term: Removal of EfOM and selected inorganic ions by NF pretreatment

endpoints.interpretation: Over 45 days, membrane permeability decreased (higher feed pressure, lower temperature-corrected specific flux), indicating inorganic scaling, biofouling, or EfOM fouling; PFAS rejection in batch tests did not change appreciably, suggesting fouling affected hydraulics more than rejection.

limitations.statement: Only one loose NF membrane type (Filmtec NF270) and one tertiary-treated wastewater matrix were evaluated, which limits generalization to other membrane types, tighter NF/RO, or different water qualities.

PFAS were periodically spiked into the NF feed for high-recovery batch tests, so the membrane was not continuously exposed to PFAS over the entire 45-day operation, which may limit understanding of long-term PFAS–membrane interactions.

Membrane fouling and scaling were inferred from permeability decline, but specific foulant composition and detailed energy or flux data were not reported in the supplied text, constraining quantitative assessment of hydraulic performance and energy needs.

matrix.value: Tertiary treated wastewater effluent from a sequencing membrane bioreactor treating domestic wastewater (contains EfOM and inorganic ions characteristic of wastewater matrices)

operating_conditions.name: Membrane type
operating_conditions.qualifiers: Described as a representative loose NF with larger effective pore size/MWCO than RO and lower energy and fouling propensity
operating_conditions.value: Filmtec NF270 loose nanofiltration (NF) membrane (spiral-wound pilot element)

operating_conditions.name: Operation duration
operating_conditions.qualifiers: Continuous NF270 operation treating tertiary wastewater effluent before and during batch PFAS-rejection tests

operating_conditions.name: Recovery
operating_conditions.qualifiers: High-recovery batch experiments to evaluate PFAS rejection

operating_conditions.name: Cleaning conditions
operating_conditions.qualifiers: Cleaning after ~40 days: pH 12 with NaOH followed by pH 4 with HCl; partial restoration of permeability

pfas_scope.value: Mixture including long-, short-, and ultrashort-chain perfluoroalkyl acids (PFAAs)
C >= 4 perfluoroalkyl acids (PFAAs) as a grouped class
Ultrashort-chain PFAS (specific identities not listed in supplied text)
A sulfonamide precursor (identity not specified in supplied text)

quantitative_findings.name: Rejection of C >= 4 PFAAs
quantitative_findings.qualifiers: >92% rejection of perfluoroalkyl acids with carbon chain length C >= 4 in NF270 pilot tests at 90% recovery treating tertiary wastewater effluent

quantitative_findings.name: Rejection of Gen-X (HFPO-DA)
quantitative_findings.qualifiers: >98% rejection of hexafluoropropylene oxide dimer acid (Gen-X) by NF270 under the pilot conditions

quantitative_findings.name: Rejection of ultrashort-chain PFAS
quantitative_findings.qualifiers: Reported lower rejection (63-92%) for ultrashort-chain PFAS in NF270 pilot experiments at 90% recovery

quantitative_findings.name: NF system operation duration
quantitative_findings.qualifiers: >45 days of continuous NF270 operation on tertiary wastewater effluent before and during PFAS rejection tests

quantitative_findings.name: Batch experiment recovery set point
quantitative_findings.qualifiers: High-recovery batch rejection experiments performed at 90% recovery using the pilot NF270 system

residuals_byproducts.statement: NF270 concentrates PFAS, EfOM, and inorganic ions in the reject stream; the study conceptually frames RO/NF use in combination with destructive treatment of membrane concentrate to achieve PFAS mineralization, but no destruction step is tested here.

study_scale.value: Pilot-scale nanofiltration system (Filmtec NF270) operated continuously for >45 days treating tertiary wastewater effluent

treatment.value: Loose nanofiltration using a Filmtec NF270 membrane operated in high-recovery batch mode as part of a pilot-scale NF-adsorbent treatment train
